notes:
Below are verse-by-verse notes on 2 Chronicles 5. Most of the material comes from older commentaries and evangelical sites. I found no Lutheran, Catholic, Orthodox, prosperity or word-of-faith treatment of this chapter, and nothing from bibleodyssey.org or the netbible.org notes, so those are left out. The closest things to "other views" are a few points of textual criticism and a 19th-century scholar's view that the Pulpit Commentary rejects.

**v. 1**
- Guzik says finishing the temple was the great achievement of Solomon's life. The verse also shows how much David did, since he designed, made and dedicated some of the furnishings himself. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-5/
- The Pulpit Commentary says "dedicated things" literally means David's "holy things," and puts the dedication after seven years of building and thirteen of furnishing. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-5.html
- Two modern evangelical scholars, J.A. Thompson and Raymond Dillard, note a parallel: plunder from Egypt built the tabernacle, and plunder from Israel's enemies built the temple. Thompson also suggests "was finished" may be a wordplay on Solomon's name, since the two share the same Hebrew consonants. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-5-commentary
- Matthew Henry says the gifts added to the temple's wealth but not its holiness, and that things once dedicated to God must never be put to other uses. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-5-commentary

**v. 2**
- Guzik says Solomon wanted representatives of the whole kingdom present. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-5/
- MacArthur notes the ark was in a temporary tent in Jerusalem, while the original tabernacle was still at Gibeon. Mabie notes the move was only about 500 metres and stresses national unity. Boda points out that the Chronicler shortens the building account but expands the dedication. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-5-commentary
- The Pulpit Commentary rejects the idea that Solomon's assembly was deliberately more formal than David's earlier procession with the ark. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-5.html

**v. 3**
- The Pulpit Commentary identifies the feast as Tabernacles, which began on the 15th of the seventh month (Ethanim) and closed the sacred year. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-5.html

**vv. 4–5**
- The Pulpit Commentary reconciles "Levites" here with "priests" in 1 Kings 8:3 by pointing to Numbers 4. It says the Tent of Meeting is Moses' tabernacle from Gibeon, brought in as a sacred relic. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-5.html
- Guzik says having priests and Levites carry everything kept to the pattern in the law of Moses. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-5/
- Ron Daniel contrasts this with David's first, wrong attempt to move the ark (1 Chronicles 13), which ended in disaster. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-5-commentary

**v. 6**
- Guzik says Solomon went "over-the-top" to honour God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-5/
- The Pulpit Commentary notes the people sacrificed through their priests. Its homily says the countless sacrifices point to the law kept in the ark, the impossibility of keeping that law, and so faintly to the cross. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-5.html

**vv. 7–8**
- Guzik says the temple was not "open" until the ark was in place, because the ark was its most important item. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-5/
- Matthew Henry notes everything else was made new and bigger, but the ark stayed the same, because God's presence is the same in small churches as in large ones. He calls the ark a type of Christ. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-5-commentary
- Mabie says the cherubim covering the ark pictured God protecting His Word and covenant. This protection over the ark would visually portray God's protection over his Word https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-5-commentary

**v. 9**
- The Pulpit Commentary sees a copying error here; some manuscripts read "from the holy place," as in 1 Kings 8:8. It takes "to this day" as evidence the writer was copying an original record from before the temple was destroyed. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-5.html
- Payne, quoted by Guzik, says the phrase came from older sources, since the ark had been gone for over a century by Ezra's day. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-5/
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown read it the same way: at the time when this history was composed; for after the Babylonish captivity there is no trace of either ark or staves. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/5-10.htm

**v. 10**
- Commentators handle the tension with Hebrews 9:4 (manna jar and Aaron's rod) differently:
  - The Geneva Bible notes say the rod and manna were taken from there before it was brought to this place. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/5-10.htm
  - The Pulpit Commentary says the reason does not appear, and doubts Solomon removed them since no removal is recorded. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-5.html
  - Chuck Smith links their loss to the Philistines capturing the ark. the Ark of the Covenant was taken by the Philistines and passed around. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-chronicles/5-10.html
  - Guzik simply says we don't know what happened to them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-5/
- On the tablets themselves: the Pulpit Commentary reckons them nearly 490 years old (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-5.html). BibleHub's study notes say having only the tablets shows the primacy of the Law in the covenant relationship (https://biblehub.com/2_chronicles/5-10.htm).
- Guzik sees the temple as the end point of the Exodus, as God's dwelling moves from a tent to a permanent building. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-5/

**v. 11**
- The Pulpit Commentary says all 24 priestly divisions served together, not just the one on duty. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-5.html
- The Catholic Douay-Rheims translation takes the phrase another way: the divisions had not divided among them yet at that time. https://biblehub.com/catholic/2_chronicles/5-12.htm

**v. 12**
- Guzik says the praise rightly centred on the LORD, not on Solomon or David, because it was His house. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-5/
- The Pulpit Commentary describes the instruments. It thinks the cymbals probably kept time and identifies the trumpets as straight priestly ones, unlike the ram's-horn shofar. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-5.html
- **Where Protestant traditions differ (instruments in worship):**
  - The Biblical Illustrator argues that instruments help the heart join the lips in praise. https://biblehub.com/sermons/2_chronicles/5-13.htm
  - Adam Clarke, the Methodist commentator, writing on the related verse 2 Chronicles 29:25, doubts that temple instruments justify instruments in Christian worship. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/msg/2-chronicles/29-25.html
  - On that same verse, Gill (a Baptist) says the instruments were David's arrangement under divine guidance rather than part of the law of Moses. The Geneva notes (Reformed) say it was not appointed by man, but it was the commandment of God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/29-25.htm
  - Be aware that Clarke, Gill and Geneva are all commenting on 29:25, not this chapter.

**v. 13**
- Many teachers link the timing of the cloud to the praise:
  - Matthew Henry: the cloud came not when they sacrificed but when they sang the praises of God. He ties their unity to Acts 2. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-chronicles/5-13.html
  - Spurgeon (Baptist), "Temple Glories," notes they praised unanimously. https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/temple-glories
  - Guzik draws the strongest version: God pours out His glory when His people praise Him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-5/
- The Pulpit Commentary follows the Septuagint and suggests reading "glory" rather than "house" in the phrase "even the house of the LORD." Barnes says the same. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-5.html; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/5-14.htm

**v. 14**
- **What the cloud was:**
  - Whitelaw (Pulpit Commentary) calls Bertheau's view, that it was smoke from the altar, untenable. He says it was the same event as at the tabernacle (Exodus 40:34). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-5.html
  - The Believer's Study Bible says the cloud did not mean God had just arrived, since He is everywhere. It was a sign of His active presence and that He accepted the temple. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-5-commentary
- **What "could not stand" means:**
  - Chuck Smith takes it physically: the priests couldn't even stand, but just lay there in the glory of God's presence. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/csc/2-chronicles-5.html
  - Ron Daniel says the musicians and ministers fell on their faces. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-5-commentary
  - Ellicott reads it as "take their places, or approach to minister." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/5-14.htm
  - Whitelaw says it filled them with holy fear. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-5.html
- **Pointing to Christ:** Matthew Henry, citing the Anglican Bishop Patrick, says the priests stopping hinted that the Levitical priesthood should cease, and stand no longer to minister, when the Messiah should come. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Ch/2Ch_005.cfm Trapp, a Puritan quoted by Guzik, says the same. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-5/
- **The Lord, not the leaders:** Spurgeon says The glory of God had filled the house, and the 'priests were set aside. Where God is, man is forgotten. https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/temple-glories Selman, quoted by Guzik, says the temple is for God's glory, not people's. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-5/
- **Application:** Precept Austin applies it to believers as God's temple today. The bodies of believers are His temple today. This begs the question, does His Spirit daily fill you and control you? https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-5-commentary Clarkson (Pulpit Commentary) says God is as truly present in church today, though not as visibly. https://biblehub.com/sermons/2_chronicles/5-13.htm
